issues.explanation: The trigger 'Arab villages' is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of physical abuse by a romantic partner and the rest of the profile, which centers on interpersonal abuse-related cues, self-appraisals, and memory phenomena. Without any corresponding threat, memory, or appraisal content involving war, military, or ethnic/geographic conflict, this item appears clinically incoherent for this patient.

issues.item: Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control
issues.explanation: Strictly restricting eating to feel in control is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The other selected items coherently describe PTSD related to partner physical abuse (criticism, violence, offender cues; fragmented/alien memory; rage; dehumanization, self-blame, emotional numbing; distraction and cue avoidance). In contrast, restrictive eating introduces a distinct control-focused coping pattern that is not reflected elsewhere in triggers, memory, threat, or appraisals, making it clinically hard to explain as part of the same formulation rather than a separate problem.

vignette:
Rangi Parata is a 74-year-old Māori man, divorced, who works as a senior editor at a mid-sized publishing house in Portland, Oregon. He came to the clinic quietly, without urgency in his voice, as though he had rehearsed the decision to seek help so many times that the actual arrival felt anticlimactic. His PCL-5 score of 77 placed him in a range of severe symptom burden, though nothing in his measured, careful manner would have suggested it to a stranger.

The relationship had lasted four years. His former partner, a man he had met through a literary circle and admired deeply, began hitting him in the second year - first during arguments, then without argument as pretext. The violence was often preceded by criticism: Rangi's word choices, his silences, the way he held his fork. The physical assaults would follow these corrections like punctuation, and over time the two became fused in Rangi's nervous system in ways he is only beginning to articulate. He remembers specific moments with the quality of photographs rather than film: the kitchen light above the table, a blue ceramic bowl on the counter, his own hands flat against the wall. Each image is complete and still, as though time had stopped to press it into glass. What disturbs him most about these memories is that they do not feel like his own. He describes them as scenes from a stranger's life, and he has come to believe this distance means something is permanently broken in him - that the self who inhabited those moments was replaced by something lesser, something that can no longer be fully human.

He ended the relationship three years ago after a particularly severe incident, but his former partner continues to live in Portland and occasionally attends events in the same literary community. On two occasions in the past year, Rangi has seen him at book launches. Each sighting produced a response Rangi could neither predict nor control: a flooding rage so total it frightened him, followed by days of the still photographs returning unbidden. He has since stopped attending industry events, which in his occupation carries real cost. Manuscripts arrive from authors expecting editorial meetings; colleagues have noticed his withdrawal from the professional gatherings that are, in a small publishing world, how relationships and reputations are maintained. His managing editor commented recently that Rangi seemed disengaged, and the comment - offered as concern - landed on him like a blow. Being corrected or assessed by anyone, even gently, now produces a visceral contraction he cannot fully explain to himself, though he is certain it reflects something true about who he is.

He has managed the intervening years through careful architecture. He avoids anything that recalls his former partner - certain music, a neighbourhood, the literary journal where they first met, which he no longer reads despite having contributed to it for decades. He has also, more quietly, arranged his inner life to keep strong emotion at a distance. He does not allow himself to grieve, to feel joy fully, or to remain with anger long enough for it to become meaningful. He describes this not as a choice but as a necessity, though he has come to fear that the arrangement is permanent - that he will never be able to feel normal emotions again, that whatever capacity he once had for warmth or sorrow has been sealed off. He has come to believe, with a conviction that resists challenge, that the abuse happened because of the kind of person he is: too passive, too accommodating, too willing to be edited. The language of his profession has seeped into his self-understanding in a painful way - he thinks of himself as a draft that was never worth finishing.

What finally brought him to the clinic was a phone call from his adult daughter in Auckland, who told him she was worried he had disappeared from his own life. He could not disagree. He comes to therapy hoping, in his careful way, for something modest: not to feel joy necessarily, but to stop feeling like an object moving through the days. What he fears most is that the work will require him to return to those still photographs - and that when he does, the rage will confirm everything he already suspects about himself.
